newsitem.title: UK: Britain refuses to reopen 14 IRA prisoners' cases.
newsitem.headline: Britain refuses to reopen 14 IRA prisoners' cases.

text.p: Britain's interior minister on Tuesday refused to refer the cases of 14 convicted IRA prisoners to an appeal court despite the contamination of laboratory equipment used for evidence at their trials.

Home Secretary Michael Howard told parliament an inquiry by explosives expert Professor Brian Caddy had concluded that the the result of tests at the government's Forensic Explosives Laboratory had not been invalidated.

"On the basis of Professor Caddy's conclusions, I find no grounds for initiating further action in respect of any of these cases," Howard told parliament. Howard ordered the inquiry after a centrifuge instrument was found to have been contaminated by traces of RDX, a component of Semtex, a plastic explosive favoured by Northern Ireland guerrilla groups.
The centrifuge, which contained about 30 micrograms of RDX, was used in analysing fabric found on suspects' skin, clothing and possessions.

"It can only be concluded that the results obtained from all cases remain a true measure of the presence of the explosive RDX, and that no contamination of these casework samples arose from the contaminated centrifuge," Caddy's report said.
Among the cases looked at by the inquiry were those of Sean McNulty, jailed for 25 years for his part in the 1993 bombings of an oil terminal and gas depot in north-east England.
The Irish Republican Army's political wing, Sinn Fein, said it was disappointed, but not surprised, by the conclusions of the inquiry by Caddy of Strathclyde University.

"The report was commissioned by the British government on behalf of the British government and for the British government, and nobody is surprised by its findings," said prisons spokesman Joe Austin. "But it won't stop the campaign to prove the innocence of these people."
A number of cases involving alleged members of the IRA have been overturned by British appeal courts over recent years.

The most famous involved the so-called Birmingham Six, six Irishmen found guilty of bombing two Birmingham pubs in 1974. They were all set free in 1991 after the forensic evidence against them was found to be unsound.
